endorsements.quote: A clinician must then approve, edit, reject, or request additional assessment, and only human-approved content may proceed to record integration and postdeployment monitoring.
Reviewer must compare AI draft against the original source or clinically available source evidence before approval
Developers should design counseling AI interfaces around clinician control rather than maximum automation.
Staff should be trained to recognize automation bias and apply the high-risk checklist consistently.
Level 4 autonomous use is not recommended for AI-assisted mental health counseling under the current evidence base.
Level 1 permits supervised internal pilot-testing with mandatory clinician review.
Local validation must report sensitivity, specificity, calibration, false positive rate, false negative rate, and review burden before level 2 use
Named clinical owner, audit trail, incident pathway, and model version record required

In supervised pilot settings, institutions should disclose to patients or clients when AI-generated draft summaries or risk support tools are used in documentation, triage, or the counseling workflow while clarifying that final interpretation and decisions remain the responsibility of a qualified human professional.

Useful features include provenance metadata, model version display, source-linked summary review, high-risk checklist prompts, edit history, reject and escalation options, and dashboards for error monitoring.
Risk scores or generated summaries should not be presented as diagnostic conclusions unless they have been clinically validated for that specific purpose and setting.

Formal institutional approval; stop if drift, unsafe output pattern, or incident review indicates unacceptable risk

unlisted_practices: Prevent AI-generated counseling summaries from automatic record integration until they pass a safety gate screening for source consistency, high-risk omission, overdiagnostic language, privacy, and required sections.
Require clinician review and documented rationale for any high-risk content (self-harm, suicide, violence, abuse) and never silently dismiss it, with escalation per local crisis protocol.
Prefer the more interpretable or easier-to-audit AI system when two systems show comparable local safety performance.
Require AI output in mental health counseling to avoid definitive diagnosis or stigmatizing language unless confirmed by a qualified clinician.
Define deployment levels with documented transition criteria and governance sign-off before progressing to higher levels of AI use.
Document class distribution, missingness, and interrater or expert review process for local labels before pilot use.

screen.reason: The paper develops a clinical informatics governance framework, safety gating, and deployment requirements mapping based on a secondary audit of model outputs and documentation, rather than conducting an empirical clinical or human evaluation.
